messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Passes the slopwatch gate clean, 257 words.

# Why observability matters

Checkout is failing for about one customer in forty. The error-rate graph is flat, the CPU and memory dashboards are green, and the on-call engineer spends three hours in SSH sessions and grep before finding that a retry loop in the payments client only misbehaves for accounts created before a schema migration.

The gap between "the system is up" and "the system is working for the person using it" is the gap observability is meant to close.

Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance. Someone decided that disk usage above 90% deserved an alert, so an alert arrives. Observability is being able to ask a question nobody anticipated, after the incident has already started, without shipping new code to answer it. Which customers hit the failure. What their requests had in common. Which downstream call was slow, and only for them.

For a team, the payoff shows up in ordinary places. Time to find the cause of an incident drops, which matters more than time to restore, because you cannot fix what you cannot locate. New engineers can read what the system does instead of what the architecture diagram claims it does. Arguments about whether the slowness is the database or the network end with a trace rather than with whoever has been there longest.

None of it is free. Instrumentation is code that has to be written and maintained, spans cost money to store, and a badly chosen set of attributes buys you an expensive pile of data nobody queries.
